bibliography.abstract: The transport sector is a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, while European freight transport remains strongly dependent on fossil fuels. Combined road–rail systems offer significant sustainability advantages, yet inefficiencies and limited horizontal coordination among operators constrain their performance. This paper explores how cooperative allocation principles can support collaboration within intermodal freight corridors in a Physical Internet (PI)–inspired platform environment. Using empirical corridor data, overlapping services and underutilized rail capacity are identified. Stylized profit calculations illustrate that coordinated consolidation of parallel services can generate collective surplus across different utilization scenarios. Rather than proposing a formal game-theoretic equilibrium model, the study applies selected allocation concepts as governance tools to distribute cooperation gains transparently and in an incentive-compatible manner. The distributive implications of alternative allocation rules are compared, and their operational translation into scheduling decisions is discussed. A conceptual platform design demonstrates how allocation mechanisms can be embedded in a neutral coordination system while preserving data confidentiality. The findings suggest that digitally supported horizontal cooperation can enhance utilization and profitability, supporting European objectives for more sustainable freight transport systems.
bibliography.title: Improving combined transport coordination through cooperative allocation mechanisms in a physical internet platform: Evidence from a German corridor

en.caveats: The findings are based on stylized profit calculations and a conceptual platform design rather than a real-world deployment or a formal game-theoretic equilibrium model.
en.what: This study evaluates cooperative allocation mechanisms for a Physical Internet-inspired platform to coordinate road-rail freight transport, using empirical corridor data from Germany. It identifies overlapping services and underutilized rail capacity, demonstrating through stylized profit calculations that consolidating parallel services generates a collective surplus. The paper compares how different allocation rules distribute these gains and outlines a conceptual platform design that protects data confidentiality while scheduling shipments.
en.why: It demonstrates a practical governance framework for horizontal logistics cooperation, showing how digital platforms can distribute financial gains transparently to incentivize operators to shift freight from road to rail.
